title: Load a dummy round under a pistol magazine's feed lips, with a sleeve loader holding the spring down
instruction: Load the dummy round into the magazine with the loading tool: the round must sit fully back under the feed lips, bullet forward. Then lift the tool clear of the magazine (you may keep holding it) and move both grippers away from the round.
context: Pistol magazines are loaded at work by police and sheriff's patrol officers (670,520 US workers; 98.8% of local police departments authorize on-duty handguns), armed security guards (California: 46,827 firearm permits among 351,170 guard registrations) and correctional officers on armed posts (380,500 in all). O*NET lists weapon use for guards and correctional officers; that use needs loaded magazines. Qualification with reloads is required yearly (Texas officers, timed reload) or twice a year (California armed guards, 50 rounds each); California's police academy teaches "Loading a Magazine"; instructors load magazines for trainees. Glock pistols ship with a sleeve loader; loader makers sell against thumb pain. Unlike holding a spring pusher back as stock goes into an open lane, here a 9.96 mm case must pass under two fixed lips 8.5 mm apart: it enters tilted from the front, slides back to the rear wall and is held only by the lips, with the follower held down through the lip gap.
setup: Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two YAM arm bases (61 cm apart): x forward, y to the robot's left; yaw counter-clockwise from +x seen from above. Bare station table. (1) Bench fixture, printed PLA or PETG (build/magazine_fixture.stl, 207 g at 100 % PLA), screwed or clamped to the table: base 120 x 80 x 6 mm centred at (18.8, 2.0), long side along yaw -60 deg; on it a 75 x 46.6 x 50 mm tower with a channel raked 21 deg that holds the magazine tube (0.3 mm clearance per side), a groove for the floor plate, and a steel keeper pin (5 mm diameter, 75 mm long) across the open side 30 mm above the base. (2) An empty Glock 17 pattern 9 mm double-stack magazine, a real factory part bought for the trial, not printed (polymer body, stainless spring; 17-round MF17017; where 17 rounds are restricted, the 10-round MF10017, after checking its mouth matches), outline about 125.5 x 28.5 x 41.9 mm, 75 g in the simulation (a published weight is 2.7 oz, 77 g), seated in the fixture with the follower on its stop: the centre of its mouth is above (20.0, 0.0), the lip tops about 12 cm above the table, and its front (where a loaded round's bullet points) faces yaw -60 deg, forward and to the robot's right. Feed-lip gap 8.5 mm in the simulation. (3) One inert 9x19 dummy round (anodised aluminium snap cap: 29.2 mm long, case 9.96 mm diameter x 19.15 mm, bullet 9.02 mm diameter; 4.5 g assumed, as published pack weights conflict) lying on its side, centre at (32, -26), bullet pointing to the robot's right (yaw -90 deg). (4) The loading tool, one printed PLA part (build/loading_tool3.stl, 74.6 g at 100 % infill, 112.7 x 28.3 x 90.9 mm): a sleeve ring that slides down over the magazine top (inside 35.6 x 23.3 mm) until it sits on the fixture tower; a roof 1 mm above the lip tips with a 6.5 x 2.5 mm tongue that reaches through the lip gap and pushes the follower about 5-6 mm down; a 4 x 5 mm tooth at its front that pushes a round's base rearward when the tool is raised; and an 80 x 7 mm fin with finger-seat lugs to hold it by. It stands upright on its ring with the point that sits over the magazine mouth when seated at (26, 18), turned like the magazine (yaw -60 deg). (5) Both arms at the ready pose, grippers open. Tape outlines mark the tool and the round. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot. No firearm and no live ammunition in the room.
scoring: Loaded means all of: the whole case under both feed lips with the centre no higher than 0.3 mm above the lip line (the height at which a centred round touches both lips), the case mouth behind the end of the lip ramp and the base behind the constant-gap part of the lips; bullet forward (axis within 20 deg of the magazine's front); tilt under 10 deg; base within 2 mm of the rear wall; centre within 1 mm of the lip line (the follower holds the round up against the lips); yaw under 5 deg. Tool off means the tool touches neither the magazine, the follower nor the round, and the point that sits over the mouth when seated is at least 72 mm from its seated position (lifted straight up, the ring bottom is then about 8 mm above the lip tops). Score 0 for the whole trial if at any time: the round entered or rested in the lip gap from above (any point of the case axis over the constant-gap lips more than 1 mm above the lip line while the case's lowest point is below the lip tops; no demo run that slid the round in from the front met this), the magazine moved more than 2 mm or tilted more than 2 deg in the fixture, or any object fell off the table. Otherwise, counted only while every finger-pad point of both grippers is at least 50 mm from the round centre (0 while one is closer), the score is the lowest level held over the last 2 s: 1.0 loaded and tool off; 0.25 the round held under the lips, bullet forward, but not loaded, or loaded with the tool still on; 0 otherwise (round on the table, on top of the lips, reversed or nose-down). The trial ends on 1.0. Doing nothing scores 0. Real trial (video, ruler, 0.6 mm feeler gauge, photo), checked in this order after the hands have stayed away for 2 s: tool off = nothing of the tool touches the magazine or the round, and its ring is above the lip tops; hands = both grippers at least 5 cm from the round for those 2 s (video, ruler in view); held under the lips = a photo into the mouth shows the case under both lips, bullet forward; loaded = in addition the 0.6 mm feeler cannot be slid down behind the case base along the rear wall, the case lies square across the mouth (photo from above, square to the lip edges by eye), and the round pressed 2 mm down with a finger springs back against the lips; then pull the keeper pin, take the magazine out, turn it mouth down and tap it once on the palm: a held round must stay in. Magazine moved = a pencil line drawn across the magazine and the fixture tower before the trial is offset by more than 2 mm (ruler); round in the lip gap from above, object fallen = video. The feeler matches the simulator's effective rear-gap limit (the case-mouth rule allows about 0.6 mm for a level round); the photo and finger checks are coarser than its 1 mm lip-line, 5 deg yaw and 0.3 mm limits.
fidelity: Isaac Lab-Arena yam_arena, PhysX 480 Hz, 20 Hz control; YAM fingers capped at 40 N. Magazine mouth, lips and follower from a hobby CAD model; lip gap 8.5 mm (published 0.34 in). Follower spring 8.3 N on its stop: estimated from one published gauge reading, not measured (another implies about 12 N). Real trials need a real factory magazine. Round 4.5 g snap cap (live about 12 g). Frictions estimated. Fixture and tool are printed parts; the tool tooth is our addition to the factory sleeve loader.
reset_notes: Press the round forward out from under the lips, check the follower returns to its stop, check the magazine is seated in the fixture with the keeper pin in and the pencil line aligned, and put the tool and the round on their tape outlines. Dummy rounds only: check each round is inert before every session; no live ammunition or firearm in the room.
